common_name: Wheeler's Variety Butcher's Broom (Self-Fertile Tall Ruscus for Dry Shade)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in spring in average to dry, well-drained soil in part sun to full shade; Wheeler's Variety came out of Elizabeth Lawrence's old Raleigh garden and is among the most durable clumping evergreens available for neglected, root-filled dry shade.

directions: Set divisions into average to dry, well-drained soil in part sun to light or full shade, choosing this selection where a single self-fertile clump is wanted without pairing a separate male plant nearby. Wheeler's Variety grows taller and more openly clumping than the species over time, reaching roughly four feet in a decade, with stiff, spine-tipped cladodes that hold up under ice, drought, and deep root competition from overhead trees. It sets its glossy red berries reliably on its own each winter and needs no supplemental feeding or pruning beyond removing old, worn stems at the base every few years. Excellent as a long-lived anchor shrub in the driest, darkest corners of a woodland garden where few broadleaf evergreens persist.

common_name: Elizabeth Lawrence Butcher's Broom (Dwarf Heavy-Fruiting Ruscus)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil from full sun to full shade; this dwarf, slow-growing form named for horticulturist Elizabeth Lawrence stays compact while producing an unusually heavy set of red winter berries.

directions: Grow in ordinary, well-drained soil in anything from full sun to deep shade, siting divisions about two feet apart since this cultivar stays noticeably more compact and slower to spread than the species. Its main distinction is an exceptionally heavy berry set on female wood each winter, producing a dense show of red fruit against the stiff, spine-tipped cladodes even on young plants. Verticillium wilt resistance and low water needs make it a trouble-free choice for foundation plantings, edging deep-shade beds, or mixing with a fruiting male seedling nearby for reliable cross-pollination. Leave old, tattered stems in place until new growth emerges in spring, then cut them back to the base.
